edges.effect_quant: In a meta-analysis of 2998 patients with iron deficiency anemia, biopsy-confirmed celiac disease was present in 3.2% overall and 5.5% in higher-quality studies; among 100 celiac patients in an Iranian cohort, 31.6% still had anemia and 25.4% had depleted iron stores despite a gluten-free diet.
edges.population: adults and children with celiac disease or unexplained iron deficiency anemia
edges.mechanism: Celiac disease damages the proximal small intestine where nonheme iron is primarily absorbed, reducing iron uptake even before classic gastrointestinal symptoms appear. Ongoing mucosal inflammation and villous atrophy can therefore present as isolated iron deficiency anemia or make oral iron repletion sluggish until gluten withdrawal heals the bowel.
edges.summary: Celiac disease is a well-established cause of iron deficiency anemia through malabsorption, and anemia is one of its common extraintestinal presentations. The signal is strong enough that unexplained iron deficiency anemia is routinely considered a reason to screen for celiac disease.
edges.caveats: The association is clearest in untreated disease; anemia can improve substantially after a strict gluten-free diet, although iron stores may take much longer to normalize. Prevalence estimates vary with age, sex mix, biopsy strategy, and whether patients are already on a gluten-free diet.

evidence.notes: Prevalence of Celiac Disease in Patients With Iron Deficiency Anemia-A Systematic Review With Meta-analysis.
